lines: Casey Morgan
+1 (555) 010-7731 | casey.morgan@example.com | example.com/portfolio/cmorgan
Date of birth: 3 Mar 1997 | Nationality: Canadian
EDUCATION
Lakeshore University | B.A. in Cognitive Science | Metro City, USA | Sep 2015 - May 2019
EXPERIENCE
Pinegrove Financial | Senior UX Researcher | Metro City, USA | Mar 2022 - Jun 2025
- Cut the card-dispute form's abandonment rate from 37% to 22% in a four-week A/B test by splitting it into three short steps with saved progress.
- Brought the design system to WCAG 2.1 AA by setting body-text contrast to at least 3:1 against every background.

- Synthesizing 60 interviews, 400 survey responses and 18 months of support tickets through affinity mapping, journey mapping and a tagged clip library, cut repeat support calls about statements by 23%.
- Presented quarterly findings to the head of product and two design teams; three of the top five recommended fixes shipped in the next release cycle.
- Trained 12 product managers to run their own unmoderated tests with a shared script template, which doubled the number of tests run each quarter.
- Led research on the mobile onboarding flow, testing three prototypes with 24 new customers; the shipped design raised completed sign-ups from 41% to 58% in the quarter after launch.
Northwind Health | UX Research Associate | Metro City, USA | Jul 2019 - Feb 2022
- Raised the patient app's Net Promoter Score from 6.1 to 8.4, calculated as the average 0-10 recommendation rating across 2,000 monthly survey responses.
- Interviewed 40 patients about appointment reminders; the findings led to a two-way text reminder that cut missed appointments from 14% to 9%.
- Writes the screener and consent templates for all patient studies, cutting study setup time from two weeks to three days.
- Tested the telehealth waiting-room screens with 16 older patients; the revised layout cut support calls about joining a video visit by 30%.
PROJECTS
Accessible Transit Map | Independent Project | Figma | Sep 2024 - Present
- Redesigned a city transit map for screen-reader and low-vision riders, and tested it with 12 participants on timed route-finding tasks.
- Cut median route-finding time from 90 to 60 seconds, a 50% improvement, by adding audio landmarks and high-contrast line colors.
- Raised task success by 20% across 12 participants, from 65% to 85%, with audio landmarks and high-contrast line colors.
Community Clinic Booking Redesign | Volunteer, Team of 3 | Figma | Mar 2023 - Aug 2023
- Redesigned a free clinic's online booking flow, cutting the steps to book from 9 to 4; phone bookings fell by a quarter in the next two months.
- Recruited 10 clinic patients and ran two rounds of hallway testing, fixing the six issues that stopped first-time users from finishing a booking.
- Wrote the clinic's volunteer handbook for maintaining the booking pages, which two later volunteer teams used to add Spanish-language booking.
SKILLS
Tools: Figma, screen-reader testing (VoiceOver, NVDA), Tableau
Methods: moderated and unmoderated usability testing, interveiws, surveys, A/B testing

items.says: The résumé wrongly includes date of birth and nationality.
items.because: They are unrelated to professional qualifications and create unnecessary personal information.

items.says: Leading with Education weakens the current professional story.
items.because: After six years of UX research work, it delays the more relevant experience and projects.

items.says: A 3:1 contrast ratio is wrong for normal-sized body text.
items.because: WCAG 2.1 AA generally requires at least 4.5:1 for normal-sized text.

items.says: Contrast alone does not establish WCAG 2.1 AA conformance.
items.because: The broader claim requires all applicable Level A and AA criteria to be assessed and satisfied.

items.says: The line does not say how accessibility was evaluated or validated.
items.because: A specification alone does not show the candidate’s accessibility-evaluation expertise.

items.says: The line wrongly credits synthesis methods with directly reducing repeat support calls.
items.because: Those methods organize evidence but do not themselves change statements or support interactions.

items.says: The 23% reduction is buried behind a long list of sources and methods.
items.because: A scanning reader reaches the business result only after processing that list.

items.says: The 23% reduction lacks a measurement period and comparison baseline.
items.because: The reader cannot tell what interval the reduction compares.

items.says: “Recommended fixes” does not identify the product area or customer problem.
“Doubled” omits the underlying quarterly test counts.
items.because: Without the counts, the reader cannot judge the research cadence or adoption.

items.says: “The number of tests run each quarter” is unnecessarily verbose.
Prototype testing does not establish that the shipped design caused the sign-up increase.
items.because: Traffic mix, seasonality or concurrent changes could also explain the increase.

items.says: The role’s strongest quantified achievement appears last.
items.because: That delays the clearest evidence of research tied to a major product outcome.

items.says: “Testing three prototypes” does not identify the research format.
An average recommendation rating is incorrectly labeled “Net Promoter Score.”
items.because: NPS is the percentage of 9–10 ratings minus the percentage of 0–6 ratings, not a 0–10 average.

items.says: The rating increase does not identify the candidate’s research work or the product change it informed.
items.because: The reader cannot tell what the candidate personally contributed.

items.says: The role’s strongest quantified achievement does not open the entry.
items.because: The drop in missed appointments would provide an immediate, consequential outcome.

items.says: “The findings led to” gives neither the key patient insight nor a clear connection to the reminder.
“Writes” uses present tense for a role that ended in February 2022.
items.because: The tense conflicts with the employment dates and may look like an editing error.

items.says: “Tested” does not show the task participants attempted or the barrier behind the revised layout.
items.because: The participant count alone does not show how the candidate diagnosed the joining problem.

items.says: “Support calls about joining a video visit” is wordy.
The opening project bullet gives no outcome of the redesign or testing.
items.because: The reader cannot tell from this line whether accessibility or route finding improved.

items.says: “12 participants” does not say whether the sample represented the intended accessibility audience.
items.because: The reader cannot judge how strongly the study supports the accessibility claim.

items.says: Calling the drop from 90 to 60 seconds a 50% improvement is mathematically wrong.
items.because: A 30-second drop from 90 seconds is a 33% reduction.

items.says: The line does not name the two conditions being compared.
items.because: The reader must infer that the redesigned map is being compared with the original.

items.says: “Audio landmarks” does not explain what was announced or how it supported route finding.
The increase from 65% to 85% is 20 percentage points, not 20%.
items.because: The relative increase is approximately 30.8%.

items.says: The task-success result identifies neither the participant population nor the baseline condition.
items.because: Those details determine who the result applies to and what the redesign outperformed.

items.says: The line unnecessarily repeats the preceding bullet’s intervention.
items.because: Repeating it spends space without adding evidence.

items.says: “Audio landmarks” is too vague to show how the feature guided users through a route.
“Redesigned” does not identify the intervention that removed five booking steps.
items.because: The line hides the specific interaction or information-architecture skill applied.

items.says: The decline in phone bookings lacks a comparison period or baseline.
items.because: The next two months say when it was observed, not what it was compared against.

items.says: “Fixing the six issues” does not show whether users completed bookings after the changes.
“Hallway testing” may be unclear to a broader recruiting audience.
items.because: It is niche terminology.

items.says: “Interveiws” is misspelled.
items.because: A visible typo in the Methods list can make the résumé seem insufficiently proofread.
